03Case study · Business Analysis

Premier BusinessAnalysis

Premier Packout handles fire and flood pack-outs and works closely with insurance companies. With its CEO, I traced where homeowners’ stress comes from, from pack-out through storage, cleaning, and pack-back, and turned it into a white-glove service.

My role

Business analyst, working with the CEO. I ran interviews, shadowed crews, analyzed a 36-homeowner satisfaction survey and online reviews, audited the website, and built the end-to-end journey map.

Outcome

An eight-phase journey map, a 56% satisfaction baseline, and a white-glove plan across the website, staff, and workflow. See results ↓

Role
Business Analyst
Client
Premier Packout
Location
Scottsdale, AZ
Partner
CEO, Premier Packout
Methods & tools
  • Discussion guides
  • In-person intercept recruiting
  • User interviews
  • Contextual inquiry
  • Session facilitation
  • Surveys (36 homeowners)

  • Presented to the CEO
02

Problem overview

Premier Packout handles salvageable belongings after a fire or flood, working closely with the homeowner’s insurance company. It removes them from the home or business, has them professionally cleaned, stores them securely, and returns them once renovations are done.

Insurance companies, restoration companies, adjusters, and homeowners often miscommunicate. Meanwhile homeowners live through fragile items being packed, cleaned, stored, and moved, with no clear end date for the renovation. Coordinating all of that while keeping their belongings safe adds to an already stressful time.

Nobody chooses to need this service, so every handoff has to earn trust.
03

Research approach

I combined what people said with what I saw them do, then checked both against the numbers.

01

Semi-structured interviews

One-on-one with the CEO, managers, staff, and homeowners. Open-ended questions like “What was the most stressful part of the process for you?”

02

Contextual inquiry

Shadowed crews in different roles: how packers wrap fragile items, what the inventory system demands, and where labeling breaks down.

03

Satisfaction survey

Post-service ratings from 36 homeowners on a 7-point scale, from severely dissatisfied to very satisfied.

04

Thematic analysis

Clustered interviews, support tickets, and online reviews into recurring pain points (delays, miscommunication, damaged goods) by journey stage.

04

Recommendations

My recommendations focused on better communication with renovation partners, a faster pack-out, better use of storage, and changes to staff management and the website.

  • 01Be clear with homeowners about timelines
  • 02Make pack-out more efficient by improving the process
  • 03Boxes in second-level vaults, furniture on the ground level
  • 04Assign a PM to each job who gets to know the homeowner
The CEO wanted a premier, white-glove service. Every recommendation measures against that.
Website

Often the first touchpoint, and it was letting customers down: missing information, an outdated staff roster, bugs, and an unused portal. A redesign should show the process, from wrapping furniture to packing glass, and build confidence.

Staff & fleet

The CEO wants a premier “white glove” service. That means a strict dress code with a standard uniform, and vans repaired, repainted, and wrapped so every job doubles as advertising.

Workflow

Jobs slowed down at inventory, furniture wrapping, packing, and storage, especially in cluttered rooms and cabinets full of glassware. Better packing, truck loading, and warehouse storage speed up every job.

05

Service improvements

Each fix answers a pain point the company itself named on the journey map.

What I foundWhat I recommended
Marketing

What I foundWork comes mainly from recommendations. There is no advertising and the website looks unprofessional.

What I recommendedPreventative content (home-maintenance tips that cut fire and flood risk), targeted ads in high-risk areas, and referral partnerships with insurers, restoration firms, and property managers.

Pack-out

What I foundSlow inventorying holds up every job and delays completion.

What I recommendedA general inventory before packing starts, items packed together by where they came from, and color- or QR-coded room labels on pre-labeled packaging.

Storage

What I foundVault space isn’t used well: boxes take up the lower vaults and heavy contents get stacked on top.

What I recommendedBoxes in upper vaults and furniture on the ground level, a weight limit per box, heaviest items at the bottom, and job-specific zones in the warehouse.

Cleaning

What I foundNo one is taught how to clean properly, the team is too small for large jobs, and old laundry machines break down.

What I recommendedA dedicated cleaning and wrapping workspace, a task-priority system, clear roles, and maintained equipment.

Pack-back

What I foundDifferent crews each visit don’t know the project, and the inventory isn’t detailed enough to find items.

What I recommendedOne PM per job who knows the homeowner, plus consistent labels: cabinets A–Z, sectional and bed parts, photos of electronics’ plugs.

Website audit

Major
  • Broken links: the “Learn How” button leads to a 404
  • Navigation: “Our Services” and “Company” both redirect to the homepage
  • Brand recognition: an unrecognizable Yelp logo and an unclear LinkedIn review section
  • Address: a PO box instead of a business address
  • Social proof: no customer reviews or testimonials
Minor
  • Staff photos: outdated; current ones would build trust
  • Typography: inconsistent sizing, especially in Contact Us
  • Company story: “25 years” vs. “15 years” of experience
  • Service copy: too vague to say what the company actually does

Staff professionalism

Premier works in high-end neighborhoods, but uniforms were stained and mismatched, and there were no standard pants or shorts. I proposed a uniform by role and a cleaner company presentation.

Uniform by role
  • GM & management: white collared shirts
  • Project managers: navy collared shirts
  • Crew: grey collared shirts
  • Bottoms: a choice of pants or shorts
Company & facility
  • Detailed, wrapped company vans
  • A deep-cleaned, reorganized warehouse
  • An office fit for client meetings
  • A new rug-storage system
  • A designated cleaning area
06

Key insights

The lowest points were the handoffs: finding help, the first day of pack-back, and aftercare.

Just over half of homeowners were satisfied, and one in five rated the service 2 or lower. Online sentiment leaned positive (13 of 18 mentions) but was thin: a 5.0 Google rating from only 2 reviews, and no reviews on Yelp. New customers had almost no social proof to go on.

13/18
Online mentions positive (4 negative, 1 neutral)
2
Google reviews, the only public ratings
5
Major website issues, from a 404 to a PO-box address
07

Results

A shared, evidence-backed picture of the customer’s experience and a white-glove plan across three workstreams, delivered to the CEO.

8
Journey phases mapped, from marketing to aftercare
56%
Satisfaction baseline across 36 homeowners
3
Workstreams: website, staff & fleet, operations
08

Reflection

What I’d carry forward, and do differently next time.

This project showed me how much of an experience happens off-screen: in the truck, the warehouse, and the homeowner’s living room. Next time I’d set up a follow-up satisfaction survey from the start, so the 56% baseline could show whether the changes worked.

09

Journey map & deliverable

I built the map from client interviews, observation of our workflow, and customer feedback, then organized it by theme to show the bottlenecks. Pick a phase to read it.

Client sentimentClick a point or a phase
Client goal

Find a contents company to pack up their home after a fire or flood.

Sentiment

Frustrated

Client expects

Reliable, professional help that quickly clears affected areas, with an estimate in hand by the end of the day.

Client pain points

Pack-out companies don’t advertise. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime emergency, and they’re displaced from home for an unknown amount of time.

Company pain points

No advertising, so work comes from recommendations. The website looks unprofessional and clients can’t visit the warehouse.

Client goal

Find a company on their own, or take their renovator’s recommendation.

Sentiment

Neutral, then happy

Client expects

A simple process, contents handled with care, and a transparent, white-glove operation.

Client pain points

Few testimonials or trust signals, inconsistent communication channels, and an outdated website with unclear process details.

Company pain points

Verifying with insurance what will be salvaged, getting homeowners to follow the action plan, and fitting the pack-out in ASAP.

Client goal

Get an estimate and a schedule.

Sentiment

Neutral

Client expects

The GM or estimator explains the process in detail, the estimate is accurate, and they know when the team will arrive.

Client pain points

Price and duration may be higher than expected, signing is complex, there’s too much information at once, and insurance is involved.

Company pain points

Estimates may need adjusting, some jobs are out of scope, and upset homeowners may have to pay out of pocket.

Client goal

Get everything packed out, from the first day to the last.

Sentiment

Happy, then neutral

Client expects

Workers on time in clean vehicles, fragile items carefully wrapped, a PM who communicates openly, and every item accounted for.

Client pain points

Priceless items handled carelessly, the arrival time missed, the estimate far off, broken items, and the job not finished on time.

Company pain points

Storage units late, not knowing the full scope, running short of materials, and scope growing without enough staff.

Client goal

Keep contents safe in the warehouse until pack-back.

Sentiment

Happy

Client expects

A secure, air-conditioned facility, photos of contents neatly stored, and every inch of vault space used.

Client pain points

Poor communication, forgotten items now stored away, monthly payments for an unknown time, and items damaged by improper storage.

Company pain points

Too little storage, too little detail in the inventory, an unorganized process, and heavy contents stacked on top.

Client goal

Get insurance-approved cleaning.

Sentiment

Happy

Client expects

Contents cleaned with no trace of fire or flood, no further damage, and a re-inventory after cleaning.

Client pain points

Boxes still dirty or smelling of fire, items not cleaned to standard, and cleaning that can delay the timeline and raise costs.

Company pain points

No one is taught to clean properly (mostly just wiping down), old machines break down, and the team is too small for big jobs.

Client goal

Get everything back home, from the first day to the last.

Sentiment

Frustrated, then delighted

Client expects

The same PM on the job, an accurate inventory, contents placed where they were, and all furniture reassembled.

Client pain points

Not everything arrives on day one, contents go missing, furniture is assembled wrong, and it takes longer than expected.

Company pain points

Different crews every time, an inventory too thin to find items, and furniture or boxes missing in the warehouse.

Client goal

Get damaged contents repaired.

Sentiment

Frustrated

Client expects

The company takes responsibility, repairs items at no cost, gives timeline updates, and restores items to their original condition.

Client pain points

Poor-quality repairs (wrong colors, chips in wood, warped glass), incorrect replacements, and irreplaceable items that can only be approximated.

Company pain points

Extra costs for replacements and driver time, unhappy clients leaving bad reviews, and hours lost to searches (five for one bed remote).
